V01-F-001: Few social institutions are as quietly enforced as the queue, which works without officials, written rules or any formal penalty for breaking it. Its authority rests instead on the watchful attention of the people standing in it, each of whom notices at once when someone tries to slip ahead. That collective vigilance explains why a queue-jumper is usually met not with force but with stares, pointed remarks and audible sighs. Such small signals of disapproval are often enough, because most people find public embarrassment more costly than a few minutes of waiting.
V01-F-002: For centuries, sailors out of sight of land could find their latitude from the height of the sun, but their longitude remained a matter of guesswork. The difficulty was that longitude is, in effect, a difference in time, since the earth turns through fifteen degrees of longitude every hour. A navigator who knew the time at his home port could compare it with local noon at sea and work out how far east or west he had sailed. The ordinary clocks of the day, however, lost or gained minutes on a rolling ship, and every minute of error meant miles of uncertainty. The problem was largely solved in the eighteenth century, when clockmakers built marine timekeepers steady enough to carry home-port time across an ocean.
V01-F-003: Reef-building corals depend on microscopic algae that live inside their tissues and supply much of the energy the corals need to grow. When sea temperatures stay unusually high for weeks, this partnership breaks down and the corals expel the algae they normally shelter. Without them the coral tissue becomes nearly transparent, so the pale skeleton beneath shows through, which is why the event is called bleaching. A bleached coral is not yet dead, but unless cooler water allows the algae to return, it may starve within a matter of months.
V01-F-004: Before barcodes, a supermarket cashier had to read the price of every item and key it into the till by hand. This was slow, and each keystroke was a chance for error, whether an honest slip or a deliberate favour to a friend. The barcode replaced that step with a scanner that reads a printed pattern of lines and looks up the price in a central record. Because the same record also tracks what has been sold, the shop learns at once which shelves need restocking.
V01-F-005: Supporters of school uniforms often argue that they reduce the pressure on children to compete through expensive clothing. When everyone wears the same blazer, the reasoning goes, a child from a poorer family is less likely to be singled out. Critics reply that children simply find other ways to display status, through shoes, bags, phones or haircuts. If the critics are right, uniforms may shift the competition rather than end it, so the case for them would have to rest on something other than equality.
V01-F-006: Many habits are triggered less by conscious decisions than by cues in our surroundings, such as a time of day, a place or an object in view. A person who always smokes with morning coffee, for example, may find the craving arrives with the cup rather than with any thought of smoking. This is why people trying to break a habit are often advised to change their surroundings as well as their intentions. Such a change works because it removes the cue, taking away the prompt that would otherwise set the old behaviour in motion.
V01-F-007: High in the atmosphere, a thin layer of ozone absorbs much of the sun's ultraviolet radiation before it can reach the ground. In the twentieth century, chemicals widely used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays drifted upwards and began to break this ozone apart. The damage became impossible to ignore when scientists in the 1980s reported a deep seasonal thinning of the layer over Antarctica. Governments responded with an international agreement to phase out the offending chemicals, and their production has since fallen to a small fraction of its peak. Even so, the layer is recovering only slowly, because the chemicals already released can survive in the atmosphere for decades.
V01-F-008: Many of the large public parks in industrial cities were laid out in the nineteenth century, when rapid growth had packed workers into crowded and smoky streets. Reformers of the time argued that such conditions harmed both health and morals, and that open green space would act as the lungs of the city. The parks they campaigned for were meant to be open to everyone, so that a factory hand and a merchant might walk the same paths. That ideal of a space shared across classes was as much a part of the design as the lawns and trees themselves.
V01-F-009: Once we know how an event turned out, it becomes remarkably hard to remember how uncertain it looked beforehand. Asked afterwards, people tend to report that they had expected the outcome all along, even when their earlier recorded forecasts said otherwise. This tendency matters most when we judge others, since a decision that was reasonable on the information available can look careless in the light of what followed. Such judgements, whether of a doctor's diagnosis or an investor's choice, must therefore ask what could have been known at the time, not what we know now.
V01-F-010: It seems natural to assume that a person in distress is more likely to receive help when many people are nearby to see it. A long line of psychological research has suggested the opposite: the more witnesses there are, the less likely any single one of them is to step forward. Part of the explanation is that responsibility feels divided, so that each witness assumes someone else is better placed to act. Another part is that people look to one another for cues, and a crowd of hesitant faces makes the situation appear less serious than it is. Both pressures weaken when one witness is singled out, which is why first-aid trainers advise pointing at a specific person and asking that person to call for help.
V01-F-011: Medieval craft guilds are often remembered as cartels that kept out competitors and held prices high for the benefit of their members. That picture is not wrong, but it leaves out the services guilds provided to buyers who had no easy way to judge quality for themselves. By inspecting workshops and punishing members who sold shoddy goods, a guild put its collective reputation behind every item its members made. A customer buying cloth from a stranger in a distant town could therefore rely on a guild's mark where he could not rely on the seller's word.
V01-F-012: Before the metric system, a unit such as the foot or the pound might differ from one town to the next, and sometimes from one trade to another. The variety was not mere muddle, since local measures were often tied to local customs, such as the area a team could plough in a day. For merchants and tax officials, however, that same variety was a constant source of disputes, because the same word could name different quantities in different markets. Reformers in late eighteenth-century France proposed a remedy: units derived from nature rather than custom, linked to one another by powers of ten. The appeal of the scheme lay in that very detachment, for a measure that belonged to no locality could be accepted by all of them.
V01-F-013: Consider a pasture open to every herder in a village, where each additional animal brings its owner the full gain from its grazing. The cost of that animal, a slight thinning of the grass, is spread across everyone who uses the pasture. Each herder thus has reason to add animals even when the pasture as a whole is already strained, and so does every other herder. The result is a field grazed bare by people who each acted sensibly, which is why shared resources often need rules that limit what each user may take.
V01-F-014: Rent control appeals to a simple sense of fairness: tenants should not be priced out of homes they already occupy. For those who hold a controlled lease, the policy often delivers exactly that, and they may stay put for decades at a modest rent. The difficulty lies with the people who do not yet have such a lease, since landlords facing capped returns have less reason to build, maintain or let new flats. A city may thus end up protecting its current tenants at the expense of newcomers, who face fewer and costlier homes to choose from.
V01-F-015: Earthworms are easily dismissed as humble creatures, yet few animals do more to shape the soil in which plants grow. As they burrow, they open channels through which air and rainwater can reach the roots below. They also drag fallen leaves down into their tunnels, carrying dead plant matter from the surface into the soil where it can decay. The leaves they swallow, along with the soil around them, pass through their bodies and emerge as casts that are richer in nutrients than the surrounding earth. Over many years, this ceaseless digging, feeding and excreting can turn over the whole upper layer of a field, which is why farmers have long welcomed worms.
V01-F-016: Electricity is unusual among goods in that, on a conventional grid, it must be produced at the very moment it is consumed. Power stations that burn fuel can meet this requirement by raising or lowering output as demand changes through the day. Solar panels and wind turbines cannot be steered in the same way, since their output follows the weather rather than the needs of consumers. Large batteries help to close this gap by storing surplus power when the sun shines or the wind blows and releasing it later.
V01-F-017: Until the middle of the twentieth century, cargo was loaded onto ships piece by piece, with dockworkers carrying sacks, barrels and crates by hand or on slings. Loading a single vessel in this way could take days, and goods were often damaged or stolen while they sat on the quay. Standard steel containers changed the job entirely, since a sealed box could be lifted by crane from a lorry to a ship and back without its contents being touched. Because the boxes were all the same size, ports, ships, trains and lorries could be built around them, and the cost of moving goods across the world fell sharply.
V01-F-018: Designers of websites and apps have learned that small choices about layout can steer users without their noticing. A subscription that takes one click to start but several screens to cancel, or a box pre-ticked to accept marketing emails, works this way. Such designs, often called dark patterns, do not forbid anything, since the subscriber can still cancel and the box can still be unticked; they simply make the option the company prefers the easiest one to take. Critics argue that this is precisely what makes them troubling, since a user who never noticed being steered has no reason to object.
V01-F-019: Gossip has a poor reputation, yet in small communities it has long done work that no formal institution could do as cheaply. Talk about who failed to repay a loan or broke a promise spreads knowledge of people's conduct far beyond those who witnessed it. Since any lapse may become common knowledge in this way, most people have a strong motive to behave well even when no one is watching at the moment. Gossip thus acts as an informal system of reputation, though the same mechanism that punishes cheats can also spread falsehoods about the innocent.
V01-F-020: When people test a belief, they tend to look for cases that would fit it rather than cases that would refute it. Someone convinced, say, that a colleague is lazy will notice each late arrival and pass over the many mornings when the colleague came early. Each late arrival then feels like fresh proof of laziness, although it was noticed only because the belief directed where to look. The remedy is not to have fewer beliefs but to ask, deliberately, what one would expect to see if the belief were false. Evidence gathered in answer to that question can genuinely test a belief, because it was not selected by the belief it is meant to judge.
V01-F-021: The simplest textbook model predicts that a minimum wage set above the market rate must reduce employment, since labour has become more expensive. Yet that prediction assumes employers have no power to set wages, competing for workers so fiercely that each is paid exactly what the market will bear. Where a few employers dominate a local labour market, they have exactly such power, and a modest minimum may then draw more people into work rather than fewer. The debate is thus less about whether the textbook logic is valid than about which kind of labour market a particular town actually resembles.
V01-F-022: Dividing a task among specialists raises output, because each worker becomes quicker at a narrow job than anyone could be at the whole. But the gain depends on the size of the market, since a specialist is worth employing only if there is enough demand to keep him busy at his one task. A village blacksmith must therefore do every kind of metalwork himself, while a large city can support separate makers of nails, locks and hinges. Specialisation is thus less a choice that any workshop can make than a reward that grows as trade widens the circle of buyers.
V01-F-023: A loaf of bread is worth no more to its buyer because millions of other loaves are sold the same day. A telephone is another matter: owned by one person, it is useless, and it grows more useful with every new subscriber who can be called. Where value grows with the number of users in this way, an early lead tends to feed on itself, as each new user makes the service more attractive to the next. The same feature that rewards the leader also shields it, since a rival must persuade people to leave the network where their contacts already are. Because such a lead both grows and protects itself, these markets tend to settle on one or two dominant providers, which need not be the best ones, only the ones that grew large first.
V01-F-024: Geologists studying rock laid down at the time the dinosaurs vanished found a thin band of clay unusually rich in iridium, a metal rare in the earth's crust but common in asteroids. This suggested that a large asteroid had struck the earth, scattering its dust worldwide, and that the impact might explain the extinction. If the hypothesis was right, however, so violent an impact should have left a crater of enormous size, of the right age, somewhere on the planet. The later identification of a buried crater of the predicted size and age, beneath the Yucatan coast of Mexico, turned a bold conjecture into the leading explanation.
V01-F-025: Early filters for junk email worked by blocking messages that contained words commonly found in advertising, such as offers of free money. Senders quickly learned to misspell those words or hide them in images, so that their messages slipped past the lists. Filters then began to learn from examples, weighing hundreds of features of each message instead of a few forbidden words. Each improvement, however, taught senders what the filter was now looking for, and the advantage passed back to them until the next adjustment. The contest has no final victory for either side, because a filter that learns and an adversary who adapts each supply the other with the lessons it needs.
